arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: The government advocate stated that the Act is a key tool for incapacitating serial offenders.
The defendant advocate claimed the government's theory conflicts with the statutory language.
Justice Roberts asked how the recidivist status differs from other sentencing factors.
Justice Kennedy inquired about statutes that use the term offender instead of offense.

paragraphs: The case tests how courts calculate the highest possible sentence for a new crime when the defendant has prior convictions.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The government wants the court to allow prior convictions to raise the maximum sentence for the current crime.
The defendant wants the court to limit the maximum sentence based only on the current offense's statutory text.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The government argues that recidivism statutes define prior offenses partly by their maximum imprisonment terms.
The defendant argues that the statutory language does not support using prior convictions to increase the current maximum.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Scalia asked why the higher maximum would not apply to a first-time offender.
Justice Stevens asked if a dispute over recidivist status requires the record to establish it definitively.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This issue determines how judges calculate the highest possible prison term for repeat offenders. It affects the severity of sentences for crimes committed by individuals with prior records. The outcome shapes the balance between punishing current conduct and accounting for criminal history.
